lesson_title: Post-test, Day 10: one item per course concept

metadata.purpose: Post-test taken on day 10's morning, after the review session: about 2 hours. Passing it earns the day-10 certificate.
metadata.pass_rule: Pass at 70% overall: 30 of the 42 items. There is no separate minimum on the written items.
metadata.blueprint: docs/build-spec.md, Marking and assessment: one item per Role Concept (Role Concepts Order, as of 30 Oct 2026)
metadata.grading: Every item is worth one point. Multiple-choice items score right or wrong. A written item is right when the answer states every point in its answer_key, in any wording; instructors mark the written items against the key over lunch and while the class traces.
metadata.pretest: Parallel to quizes/pretest: the same concepts at the same skill level, through new scenarios. No stem repeats a pretest stem.

questions.question_stem: Two honest nodes briefly hold different versions of the chain's latest block, so each shows a different set of recent payments. What brings them back to one shared history?
questions.correct_answer: The consensus rule: each node applies the same rule, so both come to accept one history.
incorrect_answers: The signatures: each node keeps the version whose payments carry more valid signatures.
The timestamps: each node keeps the version whose block claims the earliest creation time.
The explorers: each node copies whichever version the most used public explorer shows.
questions.explanation: Signatures, hashes and timestamps can be valid on both versions, so none of them can choose. Consensus is the rule that makes every honest node accept the same history.

questions.question_stem: You follow stolen funds out of one Bitcoin address and, in a separate case, out of one Ethereum address. What do you follow on each chain?
questions.correct_answer: Bitcoin: outputs spent as inputs in later transactions. Ethereum: transfers between addresses.
incorrect_answers: Bitcoin: changes in each address's stored balance. Ethereum: outputs spent as later inputs.
Both chains: outputs spent as inputs in later transactions, since both keep unspent coins.
Both chains: changes to each address's stored balance, since both keep a balance per account.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent outputs, so a trace follows outputs into later inputs. Ethereum keeps accounts, so a trace follows transfers between addresses.
questions.lesson_block: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: A wallet maker's signing code used the same nonce for every signature. Two transactions signed by one of its users are public. What follows?
questions.correct_answer: Anyone can work out the user's private key from the two signatures and sign as them.
incorrect_answers: Nothing: a nonce only orders a sender's payments and plays no part in a signature.
Only these two payments are exposed; later ones are safe once the nonce changes.
Both signatures fail to verify, so nodes reject the payments and no coins move.
questions.explanation: Each signature needs a fresh random nonce, and it must never repeat. Sony signed PlayStation 3 software with the same nonce each time, and the private key was worked out from two signatures.
questions.lesson_block: A signature binds the key to these exact bytes

questions.question_stem: A payment that paid the minimum fee has sat unconfirmed for a day while the network is busy. The agent asks whether miners are censoring it. What do you say?
questions.correct_answer: Censorship is one explanation; a low fee or a relay problem would also leave it waiting.
incorrect_answers: Censorship is shown: a valid payment that waits a whole day has been refused by miners.
Censorship is ruled out: valid payments are mined within the hour, so it must be invalid.
It is paid already: an unconfirmed payment is settled once the nodes have all seen it.
questions.explanation: Miners choose mostly by fee, so a minimum-fee payment can wait a long time, and a payment that never reached miners waits too. Name the explanations you cannot rule out. Unconfirmed means seen, not settled.
questions.lesson_block: Delay may mean congestion, not censorship

questions.question_stem: A suspect says they sent a Bitcoin payment "through the Bitcoin server". How does a payment actually reach the miners?
questions.correct_answer: The wallet hands it to a node, and each node checks it and relays it on to its peers.
incorrect_answers: The wallet uploads it to a central server, which checks it and sends it to every miner.
The wallet sends it straight to one miner, which alone decides whether it is valid.
The wallet posts it to a block explorer, which checks it and publishes it to the network.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin has no central server. Each node checks a payment and relays it to its peers until it reaches miners.

questions.question_stem: On the lab's course chain (account model, like Ethereum), an explorer page for one transaction shows: the transaction hash; "Block 1,204"; From address F; To address E; Value 2.5 ETH; E's balance, 40 ETH; and a name tag "Exchange hot wallet" on E. The explorer's latest block is 1,215. (a) Which items are the chain's record, which can your own node also give you, and which did the explorer's operator add? (b) How many confirmations does the transaction have? (c) Can your assessment say that F paid an exchange, and how sure can it be?
answer_key: The chain's record: the hash, the block, From, To and the value; your own node returns the same.
E's balance is read from the account: on an account-model chain the chain stores balances (unlike Bitcoin, where an explorer adds them up).
Added by the operator: the "Exchange hot wallet" name tag.
Confirmations: 1,215 - 1,204 + 1 = 12, true only at the moment it is read.
F sending 2.5 ETH to E is a chain fact and takes no confidence word; that E is an exchange rests on the tag alone, so Low: a lead to check, not a fact.
questions.explanation: An explorer shows what a node holds, plus labels its operator adds. An account-model chain stores balances; Bitcoin's are added up. A tag alone is Low.
questions.lesson_block: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

specific_source.reading: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

sources.slide: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
Each block on top adds one confirmation
Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: Your own node returns a transaction's inputs and outputs, but no fee and no "Exchange" tag. A public explorer shows both. What explains the difference?
questions.correct_answer: The node gives the chain's record; the explorer works out the fee and adds its tags itself.
incorrect_answers: The node is still syncing; once it catches up it will also show the fee and the tag.
The node hides them for privacy; the chain stores both, but only explorers display them.
The explorer reads a different chain; each explorer keeps its own copy of fees and tags.
questions.explanation: A node's answer names each input's earlier output but not its amount, so it shows no fee. An explorer works the fee out from earlier transactions, and its operator adds tags.

concept.name: Reading and auditing smart contracts (Solidity, Vyper, Rust)

answer_key: Create: only the owner (the deployer) can mint, enforced by require(msg.sender == owner).
Limit: total supply can never pass CAP, 1,000,000 tokens.
Move or destroy: any holder can send or burn their own balance, and no one else's; no one can send more than they hold.
Records: a Transfer event for every mint (from address 0), burn (to address 0) and send.
The owner has no function to freeze, pause or take another address's tokens.
questions.explanation: Ask the same four questions of any contract: who can create, who can move, what limits it, what it records. Then check what is missing: here, no freeze and no seizure.

questions.question_stem: Stolen funds sit in two places on Ethereum. Part one is 250,000 USDC at address S, unmoved since block 21,400,000. Part two was 300,000 USDT that address T swapped for ETH an hour ago. The case agent asks what this means for the case. Write your answer to the agent, covering: (a) whether each part can be frozen where it sits, and by whom; (b) how long the chance lasts; (c) who decides to ask for a freeze.
answer_key: The USDC at S can be frozen in place by its issuer, Circle (the contract's blacklister role).
The ETH from part two cannot be frozen where it sits: ETH has no issuer and no blacklist.
The chance lasts only while the funds stay in USDC.
The window is the time before the funds' next move.
Asking the issuer to freeze is the agent's decision; the analyst flags it.
questions.explanation: A blacklist lives in one token's contract. Funds are freezable only while they stay in an issuer's token; once swapped into ETH they are out of reach.

questions.question_stem: A user starts a withdrawal from an optimistic rollup back to Ethereum. Where, and when, will the records appear?
questions.correct_answer: A start on the rollup, then a finish from the bridge contract on Ethereum about a week later.
incorrect_answers: A start on the rollup and a finish on Ethereum in the same block, since the two keep one ledger.
Only on the rollup: Ethereum records the original deposit, but never a withdrawal from it.
Only on Ethereum: the rollup records nothing itself, so the withdrawal is an L1 event alone.
questions.explanation: An optimistic rollup's withdrawal starts on the rollup, waits out a challenge period of about seven days, and is completed from the bridge contract on Ethereum.

questions.question_stem: At 14:02, address D deposits 30 ETH into an intents bridge's contract on Ethereum. At 14:04, 29.97 ETH is paid on Arbitrum to a new address N, from an address the bridge lists as a relayer. (a) What kind of bridge is this, and did the ETH itself cross? (b) How do you link D to N? (c) Who could have stopped or frozen these funds? (d) Who received the funds on Arbitrum: the relayer or N?
answer_key: A liquidity (intents) bridge: nothing crossed; the relayer paid N from its own funds, and the protocol repays relayers later.
Link D to N through the protocol's records and contract events that join the deposit to the payment, not by amount and time alone.
Usually no one could stop it: ETH has no issuer and the funds never sit in one place for long (a stablecoin issuer could freeze its own token).
N received the funds; the relayer is only in the path.
questions.explanation: A liquidity bridge moves no coin: someone on the other chain pays from their own funds. The evidence is two transactions by different parties, joined by the protocol's records.
questions.lesson_block: Liquidity bridges: someone pays you there

specific_source.reading: Liquidity bridges: someone pays you there

sources.slide: Liquidity bridges: someone pays you there
A bridge moves a claim, not the coin

questions.question_stem: A wallet calls an aggregator's router, which sends 100,000 USDC through two Uniswap v2-style pools (USDC to WETH, then WETH to token Y). The token Y ends up at address R, which is not the wallet. (a) Who was on the other side of each step of the trade? (b) Which logs show the trade, and what does each tell you? (c) How do you describe the aggregator, and where does your trace go next?
answer_key: The pools were the other side of each step, not a person and not the aggregator.
Transfer logs show the tokens moving: USDC from the wallet into pool 1, WETH from pool 1 to pool 2, token Y from pool 2 to R.
Each pool's Swap log shows the amounts in and out and the address that received its output.
Each Swap log's sender is whoever called the pool, here the router, not the trader.
The aggregator is only in the path and holds nothing afterward: "the wallet swapped through the router", not "paid the aggregator".
Follow token Y to R, the recipient of the output.
questions.explanation: A DEX swaps against pools. Routers and aggregators sit in the path; the Transfer and Swap logs show where the tokens went.

concept.name: VASPs and KYC, compliant and non-compliant

questions.question_stem: Stolen funds were withdrawn from an exchange account verified in John Doe's name, to address W. What does that establish about W?
questions.correct_answer: Only that Doe's account asked to be paid at W; W itself may belong to someone else.
incorrect_answers: That W belongs to Doe, since an exchange only ever pays out to its own customers.
That Doe holds W's keys, since the exchange verified his identity in its KYC file.
That W is a deposit address the exchange assigned to Doe's own verified account.
questions.explanation: A KYC file ties the account to a person. A withdrawal shows only where the customer asked to be paid, which may be someone else's address.
questions.lesson_block: KYC ties an account to a person

specific_source.reading: KYC ties an account to a person

sources.slide: KYC ties an account to a person

questions.question_stem: An agent asks what a FinCEN-registered exchange holds about a customer it has never reported. What does the Bank Secrecy Act require it to keep?
questions.correct_answer: Records of the account and its transfers, kept to produce on law enforcement requests.
incorrect_answers: Nothing: the exchange need keep records only for the customers that it reports in a SAR.
Only the chain data: the BSA leaves account records to the customer's own bank to keep.
Only a SAR summary: the BSA requires the filing itself, not the records behind an account.
questions.explanation: The BSA requires an MSB to register, run an AML program, file reports where they apply, and keep records. The records cover the account and transfer history, whether or not a SAR was filed.
questions.lesson_block: The BSA makes the business keep records

specific_source.reading: The BSA makes the business keep records

sources.slide: The BSA makes the business keep records

questions.question_stem: Address A is itself listed in an SDN entry. A U.S. exchange holds 2 BTC that was deposited from A. What must the exchange do?
questions.correct_answer: Block it: every U.S. person blocks property in which a listed person has an interest.
incorrect_answers: Nothing yet: OFAC must first show that the exchange knew the deposit came from address A.
Send the 2 BTC back to A, since it may not keep any property that a listed person sent.
File a SAR with FinCEN, since that is the only duty OFAC ever places on U.S. exchanges.
questions.explanation: OFAC's rules bind every U.S. person: they may not deal with a listed person and must block property in which one has an interest. Liability is strict: knowledge is not required.
questions.lesson_block: OFAC designates; every U.S. person blocks

questions.question_stem: A sending VASP replaces its customer's name with an internal code that the receiving VASP cannot decode. Does it meet the Travel Rule?
questions.correct_answer: No: the sender's details must reach the receiver, and a code it can't read does not.
incorrect_answers: Yes: the rule asks only that some sender reference travel with the value on chain.
Yes: a code protects the customer's privacy, which the rule lets VASPs put first.
No: the sender's full name must be written onto the blockchain in the transaction.
questions.explanation: The Travel Rule requires the sending institution to pass on the required sender and recipient information, off chain is fine. A code the receiver cannot decode does not comply.
questions.lesson_block: The Travel Rule sends the sender's data along

concept.name: Permissioned ledgers: what an analyst can and cannot see

questions.question_stem: Your agency is a member of one channel on a bank consortium's Hyperledger Fabric network. A payment you are tracing used a private data collection your agency is not in. What can you see of it?
questions.correct_answer: A hash of the private data; only the collection's members hold the data itself.
incorrect_answers: The full private data, since every channel member reads all of that channel's data.
Nothing, since a channel member sees no more of the ledger than an outsider does.
The full data, through the orderer, which keeps a copy of each collection's data.
questions.explanation: A private data collection lets a subset of a channel's members read the data. Other peers on the channel get only a hash, and the orderer does not see it.
questions.lesson_block: The trace stops at the operator's edge

specific_source.reading: The trace stops at the operator's edge

sources.slide: The trace stops at the operator's edge
What each reader can see

questions.question_stem: Transaction T spends one 0.8462 BTC input from address A, a native SegWit (bc1q...) address, and pays a fee of 0.00022 BTC. It has two outputs, both to bc1q... addresses never seen before: 0.30 BTC and 0.54598 BTC. You are following A's owner. Write the hop row: (a) where the money went; (b) the heuristic; (c) what could make it wrong; (d) how sure you are, and what you do next.
answer_key: Where: the 0.54598 BTC output is likely change, still A's owner's, so follow it; the 0.30 BTC output is a lead.
Heuristic: the un-round amount only; both outputs are fresh and of the input's script type, so those clues do not separate them.
What could make it wrong: the payee may have been paid the un-round amount, or both outputs may be payments with no change.
How sure: Low, one weak clue alone; follow both outputs (or trace backward) before you rely on it.
questions.explanation: Every hop names its heuristic and what could make it wrong. A clue that both outputs share does not count; one clue alone is Low, and two outputs are not always payment and change.
questions.lesson_block: Every hop in your trace names its heuristic

specific_source.reading: Every hop in your trace names its heuristic

sources.slide: Every hop in your trace names its heuristic
Change is a guess from several weak clues
Two outputs aren't always payment and change

concept.name: Clustering heuristics and tracing patterns (e.g. peel chains)

questions.question_stem: Address P starts a run of ten transactions. Each sends a small amount (0.05 to 0.2 BTC) to a different address and the large remainder to a fresh address, which makes the next transaction. Separately, address Q makes one transaction with 140 outputs of varied small amounts. (a) Name each pattern. (b) How do you follow P's funds, and what are the small outputs to you? (c) What does Q's transaction most likely represent, and how sure are you?
answer_key: P: a peel chain.
Follow the remainder (the change) down the chain; the small peels are leads, each of which may reach a service.
Q: a batched payout, not a peel chain.
Q most likely belongs to a service, such as an exchange paying many customers: Low confidence.
questions.explanation: A peel chain sends a small peel and rolls the rest on; follow the remainder. A batched payout looks busy but is one sender paying many, usually a service.
questions.lesson_block: Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads

specific_source.reading: Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads

sources.slide: Follow the remainder; the peels are your leads
A peel chain: a small peel, the rest rolls on
Batched payouts look busy but aren't a peel

questions.question_stem: A company paid a ransom of about 12 BTC through the criminals' Tor payment portal. The ransom address R received 12.0004 BTC in two payments. Hop 1: R pays 12.0002 BTC to address B and a sliver (0.00002 BTC) to address C. Hop 2: B pays 11.9999 BTC to C as well. (a) Where did address R come from, and why is it a sound start for the trace? (b) Write the call for hop 1 and for hop 2, each with its heuristic and confidence.
answer_key: R came from the victim's side: the address the portal or the criminals gave the company to pay, with the company's own payment to it.
It is a sound start because the payment is known: the victim knows the address it paid, and the ledger is public.
Hop 1: change undetermined: no call; follow both outputs.
Hop 2: the branches meet at one address, C: Moderate (wrong if C is a service's address).
questions.explanation: A ransom trace starts from a known payment: the victim's side supplies the address. In Colonial's hops, a split with no clear change gets no call, and two branches meeting at one address is Moderate.
questions.lesson_block: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

specific_source.reading: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

sources.slide: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence
Ransom: a payment you can watch from the start
A note leads to a portal, a price, an address

questions.question_stem: In ransomware-as-a-service, who takes a share of each ransom, and why can an analyst see the split on chain?
questions.correct_answer: The developer takes a share from the affiliates, and the shares go to separate wallets.
incorrect_answers: The affiliate takes a share from the developer, and both draw on one shared wallet.
The exchange takes a share as its fee, and the split shows only in its own books.
The developer and affiliate split the cash off chain, so the chain shows one payment only.
questions.explanation: DarkSide was ransomware-as-a-service: its developers took a share of each ransom from the affiliates who ran the attacks, and the shares went to separate wallets, so the split shows on the blockchain.

questions.question_stem: A suspect who bought drugs on a darknet market says they paid in bitcoin because no one can trace it. What did Treasury say of that belief when it sanctioned Hydra in 2022?
questions.correct_answer: Market users often wrongly believe the coins can't be traced.
incorrect_answers: It holds for market users: their coins can't be traced at all.
It holds for buyers, but not for vendors, who cash out to banks.
Treasury took no view on it; it named only the market's owners.
questions.explanation: Treasury said darknet users "often incorrectly believe" virtual currency is "an anonymous and untraceable means of exchange". Markets take almost only virtual currency, so the payments are on chain.

questions.question_stem: Your trace reaches a large cluster that behaves like a service. What evidence would tell you who runs it?
questions.correct_answer: Off-chain records, such as aliases, forum posts and IP logs; the chain shows only a service.
incorrect_answers: The cluster's size: the larger the cluster grows, the surer it is that one person runs it.
The oldest address: whoever funded the cluster's first address is the person who runs it.
The fee rate: each operator charges a distinct rate that identifies them on the chain.
questions.explanation: The chain shows that a service exists. Who runs it comes from records: in Bitcoin Fog, an alias, forum posts and IP addresses.
questions.lesson_block: The chain shows a service; records show who

specific_source.reading: The chain shows a service; records show who

sources.slide: The chain shows a service; records show who

questions.question_stem: You must say how sure you are that address X belongs to exchange E. Three things arrive in turn: (1) X sits in a cluster of 3 million addresses that behaves like a service, with no label; (2) exchange E's own published list of its wallet addresses includes X; (3) your co-spend clustering ties X to other addresses on E's list, with no sign of a known failure such as a CoinJoin. (a) Give your confidence word after each step, and why. (b) A colleague's draft says "97% likely E's": what do you change?
answer_key: After (1): Low: a huge cluster and behavior alone, with no label.
After (2): Moderate: one strong line, the owner's own list naming this exact address.
After (3): High: a co-spend cluster plus a label of another kind (the owner's list), with no known failure.
Replace the percentage with a confidence word; the course scale uses words, never percentages.
questions.explanation: Count kinds of evidence, not labels. Behavior alone is Low; one strong line is Moderate; a cluster plus a different kind of label, with no known failure, is High. Confidence is a word, not a percentage.
questions.lesson_block: Attribution confidence: count kinds of evidence

specific_source.reading: Attribution confidence: count kinds of evidence

sources.slide: Attribution confidence: count kinds of evidence
A label is only as good as its source

concept.name: Commercial analytics platforms, as a category

questions.question_stem: Investigators make five test deposits to a mixer. A commercial platform's cluster for that mixer includes four of the five deposit addresses. What does the missing one show?
questions.correct_answer: Platforms can miss addresses: the cluster is a floor, not the whole service.
incorrect_answers: The cluster is wrong, so none of the platform's labels for this mixer can be used.
The deposit was never received, since a platform sees every address that is used.
The mixer must be two services, since one service would hold all five addresses.
questions.explanation: Platforms run the same heuristics at scale, and their errors run both ways: missed addresses (a cluster smaller than the service) and merged superclusters (a cluster larger than one owner).

concept.name: Explaining findings to agents, prosecutors and leadership

questions.question_stem: Explain this finding to the case agent in plain words, using the five parts of a model explanation. Malware sample S, found on a compromised cloud server, has wallet address M set as its mining payout. A mining pool's public statistics, read today, show M has earned about 40 XMR. The victim's cloud bill rose sharply over the same period.
answer_key: Bottom line: the server was likely used to mine Monero for whoever controls wallet M.
What the chain or data shows: the pool's statistics, dated, credit M with about 40 XMR.
What is inferred: that whoever set M in the malware ran the mining; the tie is the wallet in the sample, off chain.
How confident: Moderate (the wallet in the malware); High would need the pool's own logs.
What it cannot show: who controls M or where the Monero went (Undetermined).
questions.explanation: Every explanation gives the bottom line, what the chain shows, what is inferred, how confident, and what it cannot show.

questions.question_stem: Address D deposits 10 ETH into Tornado Cash's 10 ETH pool. Two days later, a 10 ETH withdrawal from the same pool goes to a fresh address, W. W's first transaction sends 9.9 ETH straight to D. Write the limits-of-tracing note for this step: (a) what the pool does to your trace; (b) what links D and W despite it, and how sure; (c) how sure the two-day gap alone would have made you.
answer_key: The pool breaks the trail: the coins out are not the coins in, so treat each withdrawal as a new start; from the pool alone, which withdrawal is D's is undetermined.
W paying D directly links the deposit and withdrawal addresses, a user habit: Moderate.
Timing alone: Low.
questions.explanation: A mixer pays out other people's coins; only user habits pair a deposit with a withdrawal. A direct transfer between the two addresses is Moderate; timing alone is Low.

questions.question_stem: A Zcash transaction goes from one shielded z-address to another shielded z-address. What does the ledger show?
questions.correct_answer: That a transaction happened, and its fee; the parties and the amount stay hidden.
incorrect_answers: The receiving address and the amount, as in a transfer out of the shielded pool.
The sending address and the amount going in, as in a deposit to the shielded pool.
Nothing at all, since a fully shielded transaction is not recorded on the ledger.
questions.explanation: A shielded transfer encrypts the sender, receiver and amount, but even then the ledger shows that a transaction occurred and what fee was paid. Only t to z shows the sender and amount, and only z to t shows the receiver and amount.

questions.question_stem: Two malware reports, months apart, describe different cryptojacking samples. Both set the same Monero wallet address as their mining payout. What does that show?
questions.correct_answer: Likely one campaign behind both samples: the shared wallet is the pivot to follow.
incorrect_answers: One victim: the same wallet means the two samples ran on the very same server.
Nothing: Monero wallets are hidden, so a wallet in a sample can't be used at all.
A mining pool's error: pools give each new sample its own wallet as soon as it connects.
questions.explanation: The malware names its wallet and pool, and those strings are where the analyst starts. The same wallet in other samples points to one campaign across many samples; some pools also publish what they paid each wallet.

questions.question_stem: What makes an NFT sale a wash trade?
questions.correct_answer: The seller is on both sides of the trade, so ownership does not really change.
incorrect_answers: The token sells for more than its owner paid, and that price is read as demand.
The token moves among one owner's wallets, with no sale and no price ever recorded.
Two people trade one token back and forth on a marketplace within a single day.
questions.explanation: Wash trading is executing a transaction in which the seller is on both sides of the trade. The sale changes no real ownership, but the marketplace records a price and volume that others read as demand. A move with no sale is a look-alike, not a wash trade.

questions.question_stem: After an exploit, a lending protocol says only its registered users could have called its pool. What does the way DeFi pools work tell you?
questions.correct_answer: Anyone could call it: a DeFi pool is a contract that any address can call.
incorrect_answers: Only registered users: each pool checks callers against a protocol KYC list.
Only the deployer: a pool's functions are kept for the one key that deployed it.
Only validators: they make pool calls and choose which users to serve.
questions.explanation: A DeFi pool is a contract anyone can call: any borrower can borrow, up to the entire pool.

questions.question_stem: In Euler's March 2023 attack, the attacker's transaction began with a 30 million DAI flash loan from Aave and ended by repaying it. Who lost money, and what was the flash loan's part?
questions.correct_answer: Euler lost; the loan was the attacker's capital, and Aave was repaid in the same transaction.
incorrect_answers: Aave lost; the attacker kept the 30 million DAI, since a flash loan needs no collateral.
Both lost; the loan and the gift to Euler's reserves were each taken from their own pools, in full.
No one lost; a flash loan repaid in the same transaction leaves every pool as it was.
questions.explanation: A flash loan is repaid in the same transaction or the transaction reverts, so the lender bears no default risk. The loan is the attacker's capital; Euler's flaw, a missing health check, was where the money was lost.

questions.question_stem: In a reentrancy attack, what does the attacker's contract do to the vulnerable contract?
questions.correct_answer: It calls back in before its first call ends, while the balance is not yet updated.
incorrect_answers: It borrows a flash loan and moves a price oracle, then withdraws at the false price.
It replays an old signed withdrawal after the contract has set the balance to zero.
It sends two withdrawals from two accounts in one block, so the balance check is skipped.
questions.explanation: A malicious contract calls back into a vulnerable contract before the original function call is complete. The balance is not set to 0 until the function ends, so later calls succeed and the caller withdraws more than once.

questions.question_stem: A lending protocol lost funds in one transaction: a flash loan, a large trade in the one pool its price comes from, a large borrow, then repayment. What did the lender get wrong?
questions.correct_answer: It lent against the price the trade had moved, so the attacker borrowed too much.
incorrect_answers: It failed to collect the flash loan, so the attacker kept each borrowed coin.
It let the same withdrawal run again before it updated the attacker's balance.
It accepted a forged signature, so an outsider could withdraw all of the pool's funds.
questions.explanation: A big enough trade moves the price an exchange pool reports, and a flash loan pays for the trade. The lender sees a higher-than-normal value and lets the attacker borrow more than they should.

questions.question_stem: You decompile an unverified contract. The output lists its functions by selector, with the storage slots each reads and writes and the contracts it calls. What could no decompiler recover from the bytecode?
questions.correct_answer: The author's names, comments and purpose: they were never in the bytecode.
incorrect_answers: The function selectors, since they are hashed and so can't be read back out.
The calls to other contracts, since their targets are set when it runs.
The storage slots, since the EVM keeps no record of which slots code touches.
questions.explanation: A decompiler rebuilds structure: functions by selector, storage reads and writes, calls and conditions. Names, comments and the author's intent were never in the bytecode, so no tool can recover them.

questions.question_stem: A victim's tokens left their wallet in a transaction the victim did not send. An unknown address called transferFrom. What does that show?
questions.correct_answer: Someone held permission: an earlier approval or permit let that address spend them.
incorrect_answers: The victim's key was stolen, since only the owner's key can move the owner's tokens.
The token contract was hacked, since transferFrom only runs when a contract is broken.
The victim sent it after all, since every token transfer is signed by its holder.
questions.explanation: An approval or a permit lets someone else spend your tokens. A transfer out in a transaction the victim didn't send means someone held that permission.

questions.question_stem: How does a clipboard hijacker steal, and where is the proof of it?
questions.correct_answer: Malware swaps the address the victim copies; the proof is on the device, not on chain.
incorrect_answers: A look-alike address is planted in the victim's history; the lure is the proof on chain.
The victim signs an approval for a contract; the approval is the proof shown on the chain.
A stolen key signs the transfer from the victim's wallet; the signature is the proof on chain.
questions.explanation: A clipboard hijacker is malware on the victim's computer that swaps the address the victim copies for the thief's. The chain shows only the victim paying a stranger, with no lure and no approval; the proof is on the device.

questions.question_stem: Across North Korea's thefts from 2022 to 2026, what shape does the laundering repeat, whichever service is in use?
questions.correct_answer: Mix or swap, cross chains, then cash out; when a service is closed, the next case uses another.
incorrect_answers: Peel chains to one exchange deposit address, which a freeze at that exchange would end.
Straight deposits at regulated exchanges in the thieves' own names, cashed out within days.
Staying on the victim's chain in the stolen token, with no swaps, through one service.
questions.explanation: Across four years North Korea's laundering repeats: mix or swap, cross chains, then cash out. When a service is sanctioned or shut, the next case uses another. The shape is shared with other thieves, so it is one line of evidence, not an identity.

questions.question_stem: The USDT contract on Tron shows an AddedBlackList event for address T last month. The issuer has said nothing about why. What does the freeze let you say?
questions.correct_answer: That the issuer acted on T on that date; why, only if the issuer or a government said so.
incorrect_answers: That T is sanctioned, since USDT is frozen only on an OFAC designation of the address.
That T belongs to a criminal, since an issuer freezes only addresses used in a crime.
Nothing at all, since a freeze is a private act of the issuer and not on the chain.
questions.explanation: A freeze is public and on chain: someone with records acted on this address, on this date. It rarely says why; the reason is only what the issuer or the government said, quoted with its date.

questions.question_stem: Your trace of a new theft follows a route like past North Korean cases: Tornado Cash, then THORChain to Bitcoin. No government has named anyone. May you call the thieves "TraderTraitor"?
questions.correct_answer: No: those names are the FBI's and Treasury's; quote them with a date, never coin one from a trace.
incorrect_answers: Yes: the route matches Bybit's, so the name follows from the trace itself with High confidence.
Yes: any theft that crosses from Ethereum to Bitcoin is North Korean by its typology alone.
No: only a court may name a state actor, so the analyst can't write a group name at all in a report.
questions.explanation: Lazarus Group, APT38 and TraderTraitor are names the FBI and Treasury use. Quote the name, the agency and the date; a similar route is behavior, which many thieves share.

questions.question_stem: Stolen USDC on Ethereum is swapped for ETH on a DEX within minutes. The ETH goes into a cross-chain swap service, and two hours later a matching amount of BTC arrives at a new Bitcoin address. (a) Name the typology. (b) Give its AADAPT entry. (c) How do you record the trace across the crossings? (d) Where in this flow could anyone have frozen the funds?
answer_key: Typology: chain-hopping (cross-chain laundering).
AADAPT: ADT3005 Cross-Chain Swaps (Hopping).
Record each crossing (USDC to ETH, ETH to BTC) as its own link with its own confidence word: two chains are two traces joined by an inference.
A freeze was possible only while the funds sat in USDC (by its issuer, Circle); once swapped to ETH and BTC, no issuer can freeze them.
questions.explanation: Chain-hopping breaks the history at each crossing; AADAPT names it ADT3005. Swapping out of a freezable token first is the Bybit pattern.
